title: Grammar Guide for the Book
subtitle: A New Course in Reading Pāḷi
intro: This guide follows the grammar sections of the course book, one by one. Each point is explained in simple words, with examples from the texts we read in class.
credit: Written for this course. Forms checked against Ṭhānuttamo Bhikkhu, Māgadhabhāsā (Pāḷi): A Compendious Grammar (Pariyatti, 2024).

topics.title: Nouns: stem, gender, number and case
topics.html:
A Pāḷi noun is made of two parts: a stem (the basic form) and an ending. The ending tells us how the word works in the sentence. For example, the stem dhamma- becomes dhammo, dhammaṃ, dhammassa and so on.

Every noun has three features:

  • Gender – masculine, feminine or neuter. This is a grammar label, not always the natural gender: dhamma is masculine, ratti (night) is feminine, citta (mind) is neuter. It is best to learn the gender together with each new word.
  • Number – singular (one) or plural (more than one).
  • Case – the job of the word in the sentence. Pāḷi has eight cases.

The eight cases at a glance

Case

Main job

English helper words

Example from our readings

Nominative

–

pamādo … saṃvattati
heedlessness leads … (Heedlessness)

Accusative

Instrumental

by, with, through

Dative

to, for

Ablative

from, because of

Genitive

of, ’s

Locative

in, on, at, among

Vocative

The English helper words are only a first guide. Each case has more uses, and we will meet them step by step.

  2. anuppannānaṃ kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ uppādāya
    for the arising of unarisen wholesome qualities (genitive plural) (Finger Snap)

In all neuter nouns, the nominative and the accusative look exactly the same. Only the sentence tells us which one it is.

    an untamed mind leads to great harm (nominative singular) (Untamed)
  2. yathayidaṃ, bhikkhave, itthi-rūpaṃ
    as the form of a woman (nominative singular) (Obsession of the Mind)

The one ending -iyā can be instrumental, dative, ablative, genitive or locative. Context tells us which one is meant.

  1. yathayidaṃ, bhikkhave, micchā-diṭṭhi

  2. itthiyā cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhati
    obsesses the mind of a woman (genitive singular of itthī) (Obsession of the Mind)

topics.title: Verbs: root, present stem and the present tense
topics.html:
Every verb has a root – the core of its meaning, from which all its forms are built. Roots are marked with √. For the present tense we use the present stem. Sometimes the stem looks very much like the root, and sometimes quite different:

Root

Present stem

Present tense (he/she)

√pat (fall)

pata-

patati

√jīv (live)

jīva-

jīvati

√gam (go)

gaccha-

gacchati

√ṭhā (stand)

tiṭṭha-

tiṭṭhati

√nī (lead)

naya-

nayati / neti

The present tense

The present tense is made by adding these endings to the present stem. Before -mi and -ma, a short a of the stem becomes long ā.

Person

Ending (sing.)

labhati (gets)

Ending (pl.)

labhati (gets)

1st person (I / we)

-:mi

labhāmi

-:ma

labhāma

2nd person (you)

-si

labhasi

-tha

labhatha

3rd person (he, she, it / they)

-ti

labhati

-nti

labhanti

The colon in -:mi means “lengthen the vowel before it”: labha + mi → labhāmi.

Dictionaries and glossaries list verbs in the 3rd person singular: labhati, gacchati, saṃvattati.

  1. buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi
    I go to the Buddha for refuge (1st person singular) (Going for Refuge)
  2. n’āhaṃ, bhikkhave, aññaṃ eka-dhammampi samanupassāmi
    monks, I do not see even one other thing (1st person singular) (One Thing)
  3. anuppannā c’eva akusalā dhammā uppajjanti
    unarisen unwholesome qualities arise (3rd person plural) (One Thing)

topics.title: Little words that follow: pi, (i)ti, eva, ca, vā
topics.html:
Pāḷi has small words that never stand first. They lean on the word before them, and are often joined to it. They are called clitics. Five of them appear in Lesson 1:

Word

Meaning

pi

also, too, even

(i)ti

marks the end of something said or thought, like closing quotation marks

eva

just, only, indeed

ca

and

vā

or

ca and vā

ca (and) and vā (or) usually come after each of the things they join, and after the first word of each group:

  1. na ca saṅkamati, paṭisandahati ca
    it does not transmigrate, and (yet) it is reborn (Not Transmigrating)
  2. anuppannā vā kusalā dhammā n’uppajjanti, uppannā vā kusalā dhammā parihāyanti
    either unarisen wholesome qualities do not arise, or arisen wholesome qualities decline (One Thing)

pi and eva

  1. jāti pi dukkhā, jarā pi dukkhā
    birth too is suffering, ageing too is suffering (The Noble Truth of Suffering)
  2. aññaṃ eka-dhammampi
    even one other thing (ṃ + pi is written mpi) (One Thing)
  3. anuppannā c’eva akusalā dhammā uppajjanti
    unarisen unwholesome qualities indeed arise (ca + eva → c’eva) (One Thing)

The quotation marker (i)ti

iti comes right after words that someone says or thinks. After a vowel it becomes ti, and the vowel before it becomes long:

  1. saṃvattati + iti → saṃvattatī’ti
    … leads,” (the Buddha said) (Untamed)

topics.title: The relative pronoun ya (who, which, that)
topics.html:
The relative pronoun has the stem ya-. It works like English who, which, that, and it introduces a clause that describes a noun.

Case

Masculine

Neuter

Nominative

yo

yaṃ

Instrumental

yena

yena

The pronoun takes the case of its own job inside its clause, not the case of the noun it describes:

  1. aññaṃ eka-dhammampi … yo evaṃ saddhammassa sammosāya … saṃvattati
    one other thing that so leads to the decline of the good Dhamma (yo is the subject of saṃvattati → nominative) (Heedlessness)
  2. aññaṃ eka-dhammampi … yena anuppannā vā kusalā dhammā n’uppajjanti
    one other thing on account of which unarisen wholesome qualities do not arise (yena → instrumental) (One Thing)
  3. aññaṃ eka-rūpampi … yaṃ evaṃ purisassa cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhati
    one other form that so obsesses the mind of a man (yaṃ → neuter, because rūpa is neuter) (Obsession of the Mind)

More often, Pāḷi uses a pair of words – a ya- word and a ta- word – to build such sentences. This is explained in Grammar II.

topics.title: Sandhi: when sounds meet
topics.html:
Sandhi means “joining”. When two words (or two parts of a word) come together, the sounds at the meeting point may change. In Pāḷi this happens mostly with short, common words that are closely linked. Three changes appear in Lesson 1:

  • 1. The first vowel drops. We mark the missing vowel with ’.
    ca + eva → c’eva (and indeed)
    na + atthi → n’atthi (there is not)
  • 2. Two vowels become one long vowel.
    na + ahaṃ → n’āhaṃ (not I)
    saṃvattati + iti → saṃvattatī’ti
  • 3. ṃ takes the sound of the next consonant. Before c it becomes ñ.
    saccaṃ + ca → saccañca (and truth)

The book marks a vowel lengthened by sandhi with a circumflex (â). In our texts we write it with the apostrophe instead: n’āhaṃ.

topics.title: Saying “not”: na and a- / an-
topics.html:
na – not

na makes a whole sentence negative. Before a vowel, its a usually drops (or merges into a long ā):

  1. na + uppajjanti → n’uppajjanti
    they do not arise (One Thing)
  2. n’āhaṃ, bhikkhave, aññaṃ eka-dhammampi samanupassāmi
    monks, I do not see even one other thing (Heedlessness)

Notice that na does not have to stand next to the verb. In the last example it stands first, and the verb comes at the end.

a- / an- – un-, non-

The prefix a- makes a single word negative, like English un- or non-. Before a vowel it becomes an-:

Word

Negative

danta (tamed)

adanta (untamed)

kusala (wholesome)

akusala (unwholesome)

uppanna (arisen)

anuppanna (unarisen)

attha (good, benefit)

anattha (harm)

If you meet a word in a- or an- and cannot find it in the glossary, look up the word without it: for asukha, look up sukha.

topics.title: Adjectives agree with their nouns
topics.html:
An adjective takes the same gender, number and case as the noun it describes:

  1. kusalā dhammā
    wholesome qualities (masculine, nominative, plural) (One Thing)
  2. akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ
    of unwholesome qualities (masculine, genitive, plural) (Finger Snap)
  3. cittaṃ … adantaṃ
    the mind … untamed (neuter, nominative, singular) (Untamed)

Adjectives in -a take the same endings as the nouns: like dhammo with a masculine noun, like rūpaṃ with a neuter noun.

The adjective usually comes before the noun, but it may also come after it: cittaṃ adantaṃ.

topics.title: Compounds
topics.html:
As in English (bookshop, sunlight), two nouns can join to make one word. In our texts the parts are linked with a hyphen.

First word

+

Compound

itthi (woman)

sadda (sound)

itthi-saddo – the sound of a woman

purisa (man)

rūpa (form)

purisa-rūpaṃ – the form of a man

The first word has no ending – it stays in its stem form. Only the last word takes the ending. For nouns in -a, the stem looks like the vocative singular (purisa-, dhamma-).

Compounds are very common in Pāḷi. When a long word is not in the glossary, try to split it and look up each part.

eso / esā / etaṃ – this, that (more pointed)

The meaning is close to so / sā / taṃ, but more definite: “this very one”. The forms are the same with e- in front: eso, esā, etaṃ, etassa, etena, ete, etāni, etesaṃ …

  1. etaṃ buddhāna(ṃ) sāsanaṃ
    this is the teaching of the Buddhas (Dhammapada)
  2. atha kho ete’va sattā bahutarā
    but those very beings are more numerous (’va = eva) (Few and Many)

yo / yā / yaṃ – who, which (the relative pronoun)

It has the same endings as so / sā / taṃ, with y- in place of t- (and yo in place of so): yo, yā, yaṃ, yassa, yena, yasmā, ye, yāni, yesaṃ …

  1. appakā te sattā ye manussesu paccājāyanti
    few are those beings who are reborn among human beings (Few and Many)

The other forms follow in Grammar IV. They are easy to recognise: imehi, imassa, imesaṃ …

  1. imāni kho, bhikkhave, tīṇi nidānāni
    these, monks, are the three causes (Causes)
  2. idaṃ kho pana, bhikkhave, dukkhaṃ ariya-saccaṃ
    now this, monks, is the noble truth of suffering (The Noble Truth of Suffering)

Alone or with a noun

All these pronouns can stand alone (“he”, “that one”) or before a noun (“that lamp”):

  1. kinnu kho so … padīpo …
    is that lamp …? (so describes padīpo) (Not Transmigrating)

topics.title: The infinitive in -tuṃ (“to do”)
topics.html:
The infinitive is the “to …” form of the verb: to go, to see, to get. It has no endings for person or number.

How it is made

1. Verbs with a stem in -a: the a becomes i, then add -tuṃ:

Verb

Stem

Infinitive

labhati (gets)

labha-

labhituṃ

bhavati (becomes)

bhava-

bhavituṃ

passati (sees)

passa-

passituṃ

2. Verbs with a stem in -ā, -e or -o: just add -tuṃ:

Verb

Infinitive

deseti (teaches)

desetuṃ

neti (leads)

netuṃ

hoti (is)

hotuṃ

yāti (goes)

yātuṃ

3. Some common verbs are irregular. These are worth learning by heart:

Verb

Infinitive

karoti (does)

kātuṃ

gacchati (goes)

gantuṃ

adhigacchati (attains)

adhigantuṃ

jānāti (knows)

ñātuṃ

ājānāti (understands)

aññātuṃ

tiṭṭhati (stands)

ṭhātuṃ

dātuṃ

passati (sees)

daṭṭhuṃ (also passituṃ)

pivati (drinks)

pātuṃ

labhati (gets)

laddhuṃ (also labhituṃ)

suṇāti (hears)

sotuṃ (also suṇituṃ)

marati (dies)

marituṃ

How it is used

1. Purpose – after another verb, “in order to”: dhammaṃ sotuṃ gacchāmi – I go to hear the Dhamma.

2. After words like bhabba (able) and abhabba (unable):

  1. pāpaṇiko abhabbo anadhigataṃ vā bhogaṃ adhigantuṃ, adhigataṃ vā bhogaṃ phātiṃ kātuṃ
    a shopkeeper is unable to acquire wealth not yet acquired, or to increase wealth already acquired (The Shopkeeper)
  2. paṭibalā subhāsita-dubbhāsitassa atthamaññātuṃ
    able to understand the meaning of what is well spoken and badly spoken (Few and Many)

The infinitive keeps its object in the usual case (bhogaṃ is accusative). Its subject is the same as the subject of the main word, so it is not repeated.

topics.title: “X is Y” without “is”
topics.html:
In English we say “life is hard”. Pāḷi often leaves out the word “is”. The two parts simply stand side by side.

With an adjective

The adjective agrees with its noun in gender, number and case:

  1. kicchaṃ maccānaṃ jīvitaṃ
    hard (is) the life of mortals (kicchaṃ and jīvitaṃ are both neuter) (Dhammapada)
  2. kiccho manussa-paṭilābho
    hard (is) gaining a human birth (both masculine) (Dhammapada)
  3. appakā te sattā
    few (are) those beings (both masculine plural) (Few and Many)

As these examples show, the describing word often comes first, for emphasis.

With a noun

  1. etaṃ buddhāna(ṃ) sāsanaṃ
    this (is) the teaching of the Buddhas (Dhammapada)

topics.title: The ya … ta construction
topics.html:
Pāḷi likes to build “who / which” sentences in two parts: a part with a ya- word, then a part with a matching ta- word. It is as if English said: “Which book I read, that book is good” instead of “The book that I read is good”.

ya- part

…

Together

yo … (who)

so … (he)

the one who …, he …

yaṃ … (what)

taṃ … (that)

what …, that …

ye … (those who)

te … (they)

those who …, they …

  1. yaṃ, bhikkhave, lobha-pakataṃ kammaṃ …, taṃ kammaṃ akusalaṃ
    whatever kamma, monks, is fashioned by greed …, that kamma is unwholesome (Causes)

Usually the ya- part comes first, but it can also come second:

  1. appakā te sattā ye manussesu paccājāyanti
    few are those beings who are reborn among human beings (Few and Many)

topics.title: Time words in the accusative
topics.html:
A noun for a time, put in the accusative, works as an adverb: it tells us when or for how long something happens. (The traditional Pāḷi grammars list this as one of the uses of the accusative.)

  1. pubbaṇha-samayaṃ … majjhaṇhika-samayaṃ … sāyaṇha-samayaṃ
    in the morning … in the middle of the day … in the evening (The Shopkeeper)
  2. yaṃ’sa hoti dīgha-rattaṃ ahitāya dukkhāya
    which will be for his harm and suffering for a long time (Sāḷha (1))

topics.title: “And” compounds (dvanda)
topics.html:
Two or more things can be joined in one compound to mean “X and Y”. Such a compound often takes the neuter singular ending:

  1. dhamma-vinayaṃ
    the Dhamma and the Discipline (Few and Many)
  2. subhāsita-dubbhāsitassa
    of what is well spoken and what is badly spoken (Few and Many)

topics.title: Sandhi: doubled consonants
topics.html:
Some words double their first consonant when something ending in a vowel is put before them (a prefix, or the first part of a compound):

  • a + pamāda → appamāda (heedfulness)
    tathāgata + pavedita → tathāgata-ppavedita (made known by the Tathāgata)
    na + patiṭṭhāti → nappatiṭṭhāti (is not established)

Only certain words do this. For example, putta (son) does not: sa + putta → saputta (with his son). These are mostly words that once began with two consonants (compare Sanskrit pramāda), so it is best to learn them as you meet them.

  1. pañcahi, bhikkhave, dhammehi samannāgato bhikkhu cavati, nappatiṭṭhāti saddhamme
    possessing five qualities, monks, a bhikkhu falls away and is not established in the good Dhamma (Falling Away)

topics.html:

topics.title: “To be”: atthi, hoti, bhavati, natthi
topics.html:
atthi – there is, exists

Person

Singular

Plural

1st person

asmi / amhi

asma / amha

2nd person

asi

attha

3rd person

atthi

santi

As a main verb, atthi says that something exists: “there is”.

  1. atthi koci satto …?
    is there any being …? (Not Transmigrating)
  2. taṃ kiṃ maññatha, Sāḷhā, atthi lobho?
    what do you think, Sāḷha, is there greed? (Sāḷha (1))

hoti – is, becomes

Person

Singular

Plural

1st person

homi

homa

2nd person

hosi

hotha

3rd person

hoti

honti

hoti can also say that something exists, but it can also mean “becomes”, and it is the usual verb when “X is Y” is said with a verb:

  1. cittaṃ, bhikkhave, abhāvitaṃ akammaniyaṃ hoti
    an undeveloped mind is unwieldy (Unwieldy)

bhavati – becomes, is

bhavati has the regular endings (bhavāmi, bhavasi, bhavati …). In the present tense it usually means “becomes”. In other tenses and moods it is often used where we would expect hoti: the future bhavissati (will be), the optative bhaveyya (would be).

natthi – there is not

natthi (also written n’atthi) is na + atthi: “there is not, does not exist”.

  1. yadi … imamhā kāyā aññaṃ kāyaṃ saṅkamanto natthi …
    if … there is no one who transmigrates from this body to another … (Not Transmigrating)

topics.title: The optative (“would, should, might”)
topics.html:
How it is made

The optative endings are added to the present stem, and the last vowel of the stem drops: labha + eyya → labheyya.

Person

Singular

Plural

1st person (I / we)

labheyyāmi / labheyyaṃ

labheyyāma

2nd person (you)

labheyyāsi (labheyya)

labheyyātha

3rd person (he, she / they)

labheyya (labheyyāti)

labheyyuṃ

The optative of hoti is made from bhava-: bhaveyyāmi, bhaveyyāsi, bhaveyya, bhaveyyāma, bhaveyyātha, bhaveyyuṃ. More endings come in Grammar IV.

How it is used

The optative speaks about something not real yet: what might happen, would happen, or should happen. In English we use would, could, might, may, should.

1. Something imagined, or “if” (even without a word for “if”):

  1. kusalaṃ ca h’idaṃ, bhikkhave, bhāvitaṃ ahitāya dukkhāya saṃvatteyya, n’āhaṃ evaṃ vadeyyaṃ
    if this developing of the wholesome led to harm and suffering, I would not say so (Abandon the Unwholesome)
  2. kocideva puriso padīpato padīpaṃ padīpeyya
    (suppose) a man were to light a lamp from a lamp (Not Transmigrating)

In the first example the first optative is the “if” part, and the second one says what would follow. The Buddha is describing something that is not the case.

2. A gentle instruction (“you should …”):

  1. atha tumhe, Sāḷhā, upasampajja vihareyyātha
    then, Sāḷha, you should enter and dwell in them (Sāḷha (2))

topics.title: The imperative (commands)
topics.html:
To tell someone to do something, add these endings to the present stem:

Verb

Singular (you)

Plural (you all)

Ending

-:hi (or the bare stem)

-tha

labhati (gets)

labhāhi / labha

labhatha

gacchati (goes)

gacchāhi / gaccha

gacchatha

jānāti (knows)

jānāhi

jānātha

pajahati (gives up)

pajahāhi / pajaha

pajahatha

bhāveti (develops)

bhāvehi

bhāvetha

karoti (does)

karohi

karotha

  • In the singular, a short a becomes long before -hi: labhāhi. A stem in -a may also be used alone as a command: labha!
  • The plural looks the same as the present tense “you (all) …”. Only the context shows whether it is a statement or a command.
  1. akusalaṃ, bhikkhave, pajahatha
    abandon the unwholesome, monks! (Abandon the Unwholesome)
  2. kusalaṃ, bhikkhave, bhāvetha
    develop the wholesome, monks! (Abandon the Unwholesome)
  3. opammaṃ karohī’ti
    give an illustration! (Not Transmigrating)

topics.title: The present participle in -nt (“…ing”)
topics.html:
How it is made

Add -nt- to the present stem: gaccha- → gacchant- (going), labha- → labhant- (getting). Then add endings like those of a masculine noun in -a:

Case

Singular

Plural

Nominative

gacchanto / gacchaṃ

gacchantā

Accusative

gacchantaṃ

gacchante

How it is used

1. As a noun – “one who is doing”:

  1. imamhā kāyā aññaṃ kāyaṃ saṅkamanto natthi
    there is no one who transmigrates from this body to another (Not Transmigrating)

2. As an adjective – describing a noun, like English “a man coming”. It agrees with the noun:

  1. passeyya puratthima-disato purisaṃ āgacchantaṃ
    he would see a man coming from the eastern direction (accusative, like purisaṃ) (The Mark of Consciousness)
  2. kinnu kho so … padīpo padīpamhā saṅkamanto?
    is that lamp passing over from the (other) lamp? (Not Transmigrating)

A participle can have its own object, like a verb: aññaṃ kāyaṃ saṅkamanto – passing over to another body.

topics.title: Verbs with stems in -e and -o
topics.html:
Many verbs have a present stem ending in -e, and a few in -o. They take the same endings as -a verbs, but their vowel never changes (e and o have no short/long pair).

Person

bhāveti (develops)

karoti (does)

1st person sing.

bhāvemi

karomi

2nd person sing.

bhāvesi

karosi

3rd person sing.

bhāveti

karoti

1st person pl.

bhāvema

karoma

2nd person pl.

bhāvetha

karotha

3rd person pl.

bhāventi

karonti

The present participle is made in the same way: karont- (also karant-), desent-.

Making something happen

Verbs in -e often mean to make something happen. They are often paired with a simpler verb:

Simple verb

-e verb

bhavati – becomes

bhāveti – develops (makes become)

jāyati – is born

janeti – generates (makes be born)

  1. chandaṃ janeti
    he generates desire (Finger Snap)
  2. sakkā, bhikkhave, kusalaṃ bhāvetuṃ
    it is possible, monks, to develop the wholesome (Abandon the Unwholesome)

topics.title: yadi – if
topics.html:
yadi means “if”.

With the optative, the “if” is only imagined – “if it were so (but it isn’t)”:

  1. yadi na paṭisandaheyya, mutto bhavissati pāpakehi kammehi
    if one were not reborn, one would be freed from evil deeds (Not Transmigrating)

Without the optative, the speaker accepts the “if” at least for the sake of the argument:

  1. yadi … imamhā kāyā aññaṃ kāyaṃ saṅkamanto natthi …
    if there is no one who transmigrates from this body to another … (Not Transmigrating)

topics.title: More little words: ci, kho, hi, eva, nu
topics.html:
ci – any, some

Added to the question words, ci makes them mean “any-” or “some-”:

Form

Meaning

ko + ci → koci

anyone, someone

kiṃ + ci → kiñci

anything, something

kassa + ci → kassaci

of / to anyone

  1. atthi koci satto …?
    is there any being …? (Not Transmigrating)
  2. kocideva puriso
    some man (ci + eva) (Not Transmigrating)

Words of emphasis

These words add emphasis. They are hard to translate exactly, and are often left out in English.

  • kho – indeed, now, as for: evameva kho, mahārāja, na ca saṅkamati – just so, great king, it does not transmigrate (Not Transmigrating)
  • hi – indeed, surely; sometimes “for, because”: na hi, mahārāja – no indeed, great king (Not Transmigrating)
  • eva – just, only, indeed: evaṃ + eva → evameva – just so
  • nu – makes a question stronger (“then?”), or turns a statement into a question: kiṃ + nu → kinnu – is it then …?; na + nu → nanu – isn’t it so that …? (expecting “yes”)
  1. nanu mutto bhavissati pāpakehi kammehi?
    would one not be freed from evil deeds? (Not Transmigrating)

topics.title: sakkā – it is possible
topics.html:
sakkā means “it is possible, one can”. It is used with an infinitive:

  1. sakkā, bhikkhave, akusalaṃ pajahituṃ
    it is possible, monks, to abandon the unwholesome (Abandon the Unwholesome)

topics.title: yasmā … tasmā – since … therefore
topics.html:
yasmā and tasmā are the ablatives of ya and ta (“from which”, “from that”). Used together they mean “since …, therefore …”:

  1. yasmā ca kho, bhikkhave, sakkā akusalaṃ pajahituṃ, tasm’āhaṃ evaṃ vadāmi
    because it is possible to abandon the unwholesome, therefore I say so (Abandon the Unwholesome)
  2. yasmā ca kho, mahārāja, paṭisandahati, tasmā na parimutto pāpakehi kammehi
    but since one is reborn, therefore one is not freed from evil deeds (Not Transmigrating)

topics.title: Compounds with hidden case meanings
topics.html:
The first part of a compound has no ending, but it still has a relation to the second part, as if it were in a case. To translate, ask which case fits:

Compound

Hidden case

Meaning

lobha-pakata

instrumental – by

made by greed

lobha-ja

ablative – from

born of greed

viññu-garahita

instrumental – by

censured by the wise

saddhamma-savana

genitive – of

hearing of the good Dhamma

kamma-nirodha

genitive – of

the cessation of kamma

  1. viññu-garahitā, bhante
    censured by the wise, venerable sir (Sāḷha (1))

topics.title: The ablative in -to (“from”)
topics.html:
The ending -to added to a noun stem is another very common way to say “from”:

  1. padīpato padīpaṃ padīpeyya
    would light a lamp from a lamp (Not Transmigrating)
  2. puratthima-disato purisaṃ āgacchantaṃ
    a man coming from the eastern direction (The Mark of Consciousness)

topics.title: Sandhi: ṃ before consonants and vowels
topics.html:
• 1. Before a consonant, ṃ takes the nasal of that consonant’s group (ṅ before k, g; ñ before c, j; n before t, d; m before p, b).
    yaṃ + ca → yañca
    viññāṇaṃ + ti → viññāṇan’ti
    eka-dhammaṃ + pi → eka-dhammampi
  • 2. ṃ never stands between two vowels. Before a vowel it becomes m.
    etaṃ + atthaṃ → etamatthaṃ
    evaṃ + eva → evameva

  3. cattāro’me = cattāro + ime
    these four (Lesson 4)

topics.title: The absolutive in -tvā and -ya (“having done”)
topics.html:
This form means “having done” something. It has no endings – it never changes. The book calls it the “gerund”; it is also called the absolutive.

-tvā (or -tvāna)

1. Verbs with a stem in -a: the a becomes i, as in the infinitive: labhati → labhitvā, bhavati → bhavitvā, garahati → garahitvā.

2. Verbs with a stem in -e: add -tvā directly: neti → netvā, deseti → desetvā.

3. Other verbs: -tvā is added to the root, which often changes:

Verb

Absolutive

karoti (does)

katvā

gacchati (goes)

gantvā

suṇāti (hears)

sutvā

pivati (drinks)

pitvā

passati (sees)

disvā

deti (gives)

datvā

jānāti (knows)

ñatvā / jānitvā

labhati (gets)

laddhā (also labhitvā)

-ya

Verbs with a prefix often use -ya instead:

Verb

Absolutive

pariyādiyati (takes over)

pariyādāya – having overpowered

pajahati (abandons)

pahāya – having abandoned

How it is used

It shows an action that happens before the main verb, done by the same person. Translate “having done X, he …” or “he does X and …”:

  1. āyuṃ kho pana datvā āyussa bhāginī hoti
    having given long life, she has a share in long life (Lesson 4)
  2. attānaṃ upamaṃ katvā, na haneyya na ghātaye
    having made oneself the example, one should not kill nor cause to kill (Dhammapada 129)
  3. purisassa cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhati
    having overpowered the mind of a man, it remains (= it obsesses his mind) (Obsession of the Mind)

Like a verb, the absolutive can have its own object: attānaṃ upamaṃ katvā.

topics.title: The present participle in -māna and -āna
topics.html:
Besides -nt- (Grammar III), there is a second present participle in -māna, added to the present stem:

Verb

-māna participle

gacchati (goes)

gacchamāna – going

uppajjati (arises)

uppajjamāna – arising

bhāsati (speaks)

bhāsamāna – speaking, reciting

deseti (teaches)

desayamāna – teaching (-e becomes -aya)

It is often called the “middle” participle, but in practice it means the same as the -nt form: gacchanto or gacchamāno – going.

A few verbs have -āna instead: anupādiyāno – not clinging; sampajāno – fully aware.

These participles take the endings of adjectives in -a, and can be used as nouns (“one who …”) or as adjectives:

  1. bahumpi ce sahitaṃ bhāsamāno
    even if reciting many of the texts (Dhammapada 19)
  2. sammappajāno suvimutta-citto anupādiyāno
    fully understanding, with mind well freed, not clinging (Dhammapada 20)

topics.title: Feminine participles in -ī and -ā
topics.html:
When a participle describes a woman, or means “she who …”:

  • the -nt participle takes -ī, like nadī: dentī – she who gives; karontī – she who does;
  • the -māna participle takes -ā, like sālā: gacchamānā – she who goes.
  1. bhojanaṃ, Suppavāse, dentī ariya-sāvikā
    Suppavāsā, a noble woman disciple who gives a meal (Lesson 4)

topics.title: More optative endings
topics.html:
Besides the endings in Grammar III, the optative has some shorter endings:

Person

Singular

Plural

-e

-ema (-eyyāmhe)

2nd person

-etha (-eyyavho)

3rd person

-e (-etha)

(-eraṃ)

The endings in brackets are called “middle” endings, but the meaning is the same.

  1. na bhaje pāpake mitte
    one should not associate with bad friends (-e) (Dhammapada 78)
  2. bhajetha mitte kalyāṇe
    one should associate with good friends (-etha) (Dhammapada 78)
  3. na haneyya na ghātaye
    one should not kill nor cause to kill (-e) (Dhammapada 129)

topics.title: sabba (all) and para (other)
topics.html:
sabba (all) and para (other) take the endings of the pronouns (te, tesaṃ …), not of the nouns: sabbe (all, masculine plural), sabbāni (neuter), sabbā (feminine), sabbesaṃ (of all), paresaṃ (of others).

  1. sabbe tasanti daṇḍassa
    all tremble at the rod (Dhammapada 129)
  2. sabbesaṃ jīvitaṃ piyaṃ
    life is dear to all (Dhammapada 130)
  3. gopo’va gāvo gaṇayaṃ paresaṃ
    like a cowherd counting the cattle of others (Dhammapada 19)

topics.title: iva / ’va – like, as
topics.html:
iva means “like, as”. It is used in comparisons, and it comes after the word it compares. It usually appears in its short form ’va:

  1. gopo’va gāvo gaṇayaṃ paresaṃ
    like a cowherd counting the cattle of others (gopo + iva) (Dhammapada 19)

’va can also be a short form of eva (just, indeed): ete’va sattā = ete eva sattā (Few and Many). Context tells us which one it is.

topics.title: ce – if
topics.html:
ce is another word for “if”. It is a clitic, so it never stands first: it comes after the first word of its clause.

  1. bahumpi ce sahitaṃ bhāsamāno … na bhāgavā sāmaññassa hoti
    even if he recites many of the texts …, he has no share in the recluse’s life (Dhammapada 19)
  2. appampi ce sahitaṃ bhāsamāno … sa bhāgavā sāmaññassa hoti
    even if he recites few of the texts …, he has a share in the recluse’s life (Dhammapada 20)

With the optative, ce describes something imagined. The optative of atthi is useful here: assaṃ – I would be; assa (or siyā) – he / she would be; assu – they would be.
